analytic.title: Overhead Effects in Real-time Preemptive Schedules

div.p: The hard real-time schedulability of dependent taskgraphs is studied for single bus homogeneous multiprocessor systems. A model which includes interrupts and context switching as well as bus contention is developed. The model captures real-time operating system effects aimed at realistically modeling both intra-processor and inter-processor communications. A robust scheduler is used to msess the impact of interrupt service time (ET) and context switching time (CST) on schedulability. For the class of task-graphs studied, it is shown that schedulability iS a nonlinear function of only the weighted sum of IST and CST.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A system of communicating processors is many times used as a means to meet real-time processing demands. Often times, each processor uses a preemptively scheduled realtime operating system (RTOS), where overhead activities such as context switching and intermpt servicing become a necessary component of task management and execution. However, the adverse impact of these overheads on the preemptive scheduling of real-time systems is well recognized [l, 10, 131. While context switching time and interrupt servicing time are generally designed to be small for embedded processors [5, 91 executing real-time operating systems (RTOS) [4, 7, 8, 141, they are nonetheless present.

Most scheduling studies, especially those in the hard real-time regime, completely ignore realistic system overheads since they would he difficult or impossible to include. There have been several exceptions, for example a method for computing the worst-case delay of a task executed on a system which has regularly appearing scheduling interrupts (called scheduling ticks) has been achieved [l]. However, it was assumed that the tasks to he scheduled were independent and hence earliest deadline first scheduling (a variant of rate monotonic scheduling) is optimal [6]. Another prior real-time study regarding dependent tasks did include the effects of interrupt service time for d e pendent task sets hut context switching was not considered at all [ll]. Furthermore, this work assumed that interrupts made on behalf of data arrivals could he 'custom designed' on an individual basis which may require a more complex system implementation.

This effort aims to explore the impact of finite context switching times and interrupt service times on the scheduling of hard real-time dependent tasks (represented as a set of task-graphs). It is assumed that the inter-task dependencies are due to data dependencies, and hence graph arc8 represent data transmittals. A model for a preemptively scheduled multi-processor system is presented in the next section. This is followed by a description of the allocation and scheduling technique and then by results and conclusions.

div.head: System Model
div.p: The ultimate aim of the system model is to provide a highlevel model for a statically allocated and scheduled multiprocessor system which employs a preemptive RTOS for each processing element (PE). While the model is highlevel, it must still accurately capture realistic system efFects. The final goal is to study the effects of context switching time (CST) and interrupt service time (IST) on schedulabrlity, which is the rate of schedulahle problems (for some underlying input class). While context switching and interrupt handling is a function of individual PES, such effects must be considered in a manner consistent with inter-PE communication as well.

In order to focus on processor-bound overheads, a simple hut accurate inter-PE communication model is used. It is assumed that the PES are interconnected via a single, shared bus and that inker-PE tasks communicate with shared-object semantics [14]. Figure 1 shows a model of t y p i d hardware, where each PE is comprised of a processor, memory and communication controller. Since a static scheduling will he used, inter-task communication types (either inter-PE or intra-PE) are known at initialization and thus each data transmittal is hown to be either intra-or inter-PE. Furthermore, since data transmittals occur h e tween a single source and single consumer in task-graphs, a globally shared memory (i.e. multiprocessing) approach would add unnecessary resource contention and would be Bus usage (time) is a function of the amount of data being transmitted and the data rate of the bus and these inter-PE communication transactions may be viewed as 'communication tasks.'

div.head: PE PE
div.p: To illustrate the concept of communication tasks, the task-graph in Figure 2.A is augmented to that of Figure 2.B by converting each graph arc (a data transmittal) to a communication task (shown as grey) with a runtime equal to the data-size of the arc divided hy the data rate of the bus. In the ensuing allocation and scheduling problem, communication tasks are, of course, constrained to the bus resource. The arc8 in the augmented graph, which is that actually used by the allocation/scheduling tools, can now be truly considered 'ideal. ' In a physical view, the sending task initiates a bus transf e y w i t h proper consideration of bus contention-ausing an interrupt to occur on the receiving PE. The interrupt service routine (ISR) activated by this data transmittal must place the incoming data in memory and indicate its availability (via a local semaphore), and determine if this data arrival causes the task receiving the data to become mady.

If so, the ISR moves that task to the ready list and the RTOS will then potentially preempt the currently executing task based upon priority. It is assumed that out-going data is sent (if necessary) at the conclusion of each task and that the ordering these is controllable.

Controlling the ordering of fan-out data transmittal is is consistent with, for example, the FIFO message queues of VxWorks [14]. The model further assumes that intra-PE communication takes no time. This too is consistent with a modern RTOS-for example, VxWorks provides a single, non-pagedtnon-virtual (but these are options) address space for all tasks executing on a PE, Therefore data results being created and consumed on a single P E may reside in local memory accessible by both tasks. At task conclusion only a simple semaphore setting is required, as well as the possible movement of a task to the ready list, both of these operations can be done extremely quickly.

div.p: The effort here will investigate the schedulahility impact for various settings for IST and CST. Of course, particular values for these are dependent on the particular hardware choice. However, for the purposes of the study here (and with respect to the model presented), clearly only their dues relative to each other and to task runtimes is of importance and not their absolute measure.

In summary, this model can he seen to he consistent with, for example, a bus interconnected set of processors each running the VxWorks RTOS [14]. The model described accurately reflects its features and capabilities, including: preemptive multitasking with 256 priority levels, non-interruptable ISRS, a single address space for tasks on each PE, shared memory addressing and semaphores, etc. Although Vx-Works supports round-robin time slicing of ready tasks which have eguol priorities, we assume that all tasks executing on a P E have distinct priority levels-if this were not the case (e.g. an insufficient number of priority levels were available) then the model would have to include this feature. Since we a m designing static schedules, the only time this would become problematic is if it was impossible to set task priorities in a distinct manner for tasks which could possibility reside on the ready list at the same t i m e t h i s issue would only occur for very large problem sets.

div.head: Scheduling Procedure
div.p: We would like to assess the impact of various values for IST and CST on the schedulahility for task sets. Since the scheduling of dependent tasks in a resource-constrained manner is readily recognized as being NP-complete, obtaining 'absolute' schedulahility values for non-trivial task sets is impossible. Therefore schedulahility must he obtained in the context of a particular design procedure and, since absolute schedulahility is unobtainable anyway, viewing schedulability in the context of a strong scheduler is actually more relevant.

Since the focus is on the impact of system overheads on schedulahility, and since complete algorithmic details of the scheduling procedure are described elsewhere [12], only a summary of the method is presented here. Hard real-time task-graphs are to he scheduled on a given number of equivalent PES (a homogeneous allocation/scheduling problem). Initialization consists of a random allocation and priority assignment of each task in the task graph (cf. Fig. 4 for an example task-graph set), establishing an initial configuration (the total mapping of all tasks to PES and task priority settings). Next, an iterative improvement technique is used. Each step of the iterative improvement falls into one of two categories: (i) an utilization update; or (ii) a Speed update. The configuration at each update is monitored to avoid re- peated configurations.

An utilization update occurs whenever a P E or the bus is over utilized. I f a P E is the most over-utilized, the largest task currently allocated to it is reallocated to the least utilized PE. If the bus is over utilized, a dudemag step is performed. For one of the largest bus utilizations, the sending and receiving tasks are clustered-re-allocated to the same PE. For example, in the context of Figure 3 suppose that the bus were over-utilized and that TO,^ were the largest user If there is no over utilization, a schedule analysis is performed in a manner consistent with the model described in the previous section. If all deadlines are met, then a successful schedule has been found, otherwise the recursive routine Speed is used to modify the configuration making use of the current schedule analysis. Each task has an 'as-late-aspossible' (alap) end-time, which is the latest time that the task can complete such that all deadlines can he met (the alap end-time is computed once using simple graph methods

div.head: [Z]
div.p: ). The earliest starting task which misses it's alap deadline then becomes the argument in the list of tasks given to Speed.

Speed attempts to improve the ending time for the list of tasks given it in a recursive manner. In the context of the current schedule, possible reallocation and re-prioritization of the task with the latest end-time is considered. For each possible re-allocation, an end-time estimate for the tasks on the list is computed. If this estimate is within alap end-times, the re-allocation/re-prioritization is accepted and control returns to the iterative improvement loop. Otherwise Speed recurses to the list of tasks which are the predecessors to the tasks on the current list (the recursion terminates when this list is empty in which case a random reallocation/re-prioritization of tasks examined is made and control passes hack to the iterative loop).

Note that Speed is alterately examining lists of actual task-graph tasks and communication tasks. Making use of Figure 2.B for illustration, if T5 were the first argument to Speed, then the sequence of future arguments would he: {T2,5, 2'3.5, T4,5}, {Tz, 2'3, T4}, {%,a, T u , 2'1,3}, and,finally {TO, T I } . As discussed, at each step in this recursion task re-allocation/prioritization is considered to achieve an improved end-time estimated for all tasks on the list.

Since a single bus is assumed, re-allocation of communication tasks is not possible, in this case only reordering of communication tasks-within the limit of reordering communication tasks resulting from a single task's fan-out-is considered. The net effect of this approach is that scheduling improvements on a level-by-level basis within the complete fan-in space of the task which first missed it's alap deadline are examined. Since (reallocation/re-prioritization) changes to only a single task axe done at each iterative step, this procedure can he classified as a 'one-at-a-time' optimization. While such a technique would generally he ineffective in solving NP-hard/NP-complete problems, note that random steps are interspersed with the 'local' optimization procedure whenever it fails to find an (expected) improved configuration-the net effect IS that the method effectively explores an important local design space hut relies on a raudom move when caught in local minima.

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: It is interesting to consider the implications of these results; although conclusions are pertinent to the data sets used here, it is not unreasonable to extend the conclusions to the more general case. The observation that schedulahility remains a function only of the weighted sum of IST and CST with the scheduling transition region irrespective of deadline slack is surprising. The shifl of the scheduling transition region with loosening deadlines is, of course, expected. But the region also expands (as witnessed by the increased width) implying that, as deadlines loosen, there are more trade-offs available to the scheduler. This, too, might be expected-the tight deadlines cause a more abrupt scheduling transition. However even though additional scheduling trade-offs are available as deadlines loosen, the relative importance between IST and CST remains the same (as witnessed hy the constant -1.8 scheduling contour line slope irrespective of deadline slack).
